pages.title: Start here: how this workspace runs

text.text: A ten-minute tour of the grants office in this workspace. Share it with the grants manager, the program director, the finance manager and the executive director.
: every foundation, agency and company you have or want a relationship with, what they fund, their cycle, typical grant, the totals asked and awarded, and your win rate with them.
: every request from research to decision, with the letter of inquiry date, deadline, ask, award, required match, restrictions and spending to date.
: the approved budget of each award, line by line, with what is spent and what is left.
: every report and site visit owed, the numbers each must cover, its author and due date.
: calls, meetings and site visits with funders.
The first Monday: deadlines and reports due in the next 30 days.
Mid-month: finance updates spending on every budget line.
Through the month: drafting, reviews and submissions, always two days early.
Month end: the director reviews the Dashboard with the board treasurer.
Every Monday: overdue and this week's reports and deadlines
Every month: budget lines updated, grants ending soon flagged for renewal
Every quarter: new funders researched, win rates reviewed
Every year: the ready file refreshed after the audit

The grants manager owns the calendar and the writing. The program director supplies the numbers and stories. The finance manager owns budgets and financial reports. The executive director signs, calls funders and hosts site visits.

Rename programs, categories and report kinds to match your organization and delete the sample rows once your own are in. Edit any cell in place and drag cards between columns; every total and win rate updates by itself.

text.text: A strong application is mostly done before the funder's form opens. Keep a ready file, start six weeks out, and never submit on the last day.
Read the guidelines twice. Write in the grant's notes the three things this funder cares about most, in their words.
If the funder asks for a
. Send the letter, and only draft the full proposal when they invite one.
Call the program officer if they take calls. Ask whether your project fits; it saves weeks when the answer is no.
Agree the budget with the finance manager, including any
the funder requires you to raise from others.
Keep these current all year so no application waits on them:
Mission statement and a one-paragraph history
This year's operating budget and last year's actuals
Most recent audit or financial review, and the tax-exempt letter
Program numbers: people served, sessions held, outcomes
Two or three short stories, with permission, and photos
Lead with the need and the people, not with your organization.
Make the outcomes measurable: "120 students complete twelve weeks of clay" beats "students will grow".
The budget and the narrative must tell the same story: every line in one appears in the other.
Ask for an amount that fits the funder's
Narrative reviewed by someone who did not write it
Submit at least two days early; portals slow down on deadline day. Set the grant to
, write the expected decision date, and add a thank-you note to the program officer to your Conversations.

The State Arts Board's access grant is due next week. The grants manager drafted from the ready file, the program director added this year's school numbers, and finance confirmed the $20,000 match. The executive director signs on Monday, and it goes in Tuesday, three days early.
Every award comes with promises: reports, spending rules and sometimes a site visit. Funders renew organizations that report on time and honestly. This page is how you never miss one.

Say plainly what did not go to plan and what you changed. Funders trust honesty far more than perfect results.
Reports due in the next 30 days have an author and a draft date
Grants ending in the next 90 days: renewal conversation booked
Treat a site visit like a class open house: let the funder see the program running, meet a participant or teacher, and leave with one page of numbers.

The studio classes grant asks for a six-month narrative. The grants manager opens the report, sees it must cover enrollment and attendance, pulls 118 students and 91 percent attendance from the class records, adds a story from a teaching artist, and submits it four days early. Finance's report follows two weeks later from the budget lines.
Good grant research finds funders who already give to work like yours, in your area, at the size you need. Spend your time on the few who fit rather than the many who might.
Funders that support organizations like yours nearby: read the annual reports and grant lists of similar groups.
Your community foundation's open programs and its donor-advised funds.
Your state arts board and city cultural office for government grants.
Banks and large local employers with community giving programs.
Foundations' public tax filings, which list every grant they made, to whom and for how much.
